extracted.intended_audience: writers of fantasy and science fiction (worldbuilders, speculative fiction authors)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for creating believable, non-stereotyped non-human races (species) in fantasy and science fiction stories, focusing on cultural, physiological, and narrative choices that make them serve the story. Emphasizes avoiding coded stereotyping, giving cultures depth, and choosing what to show vs. what to keep off-page.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid coding aliens after Earth races / othering
rubrics_metrics.description: Be aware you'll subconsciously code creations after people who are 'other' to you; avoid mapping Earth racial/ethnic characteristics onto your alien races.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is both fraught and inescapable, but you should research and put in effort rather than relying on stereotypes. The hosts cite George Lucas’s prequels as an example of dangerous coding (a merchant coded as Jewish). There is a whole 'Writing the Other' series recommended for deeper work; give yourself permission to try but do the research and accept you may get it wrong sometimes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make aliens function as people who can tell the story
rubrics_metrics.description: Design aliens so they can act, feel, and relate in ways that drive the narrative—not just a set of gimmicky superpowers or a visual design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on making them 'people' in the narrative sense: they need recognizable motivations and agency so the story can be told without excessive exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ask: how does this alien see the world differently, and is that important?
rubrics_metrics.description: Primary design question: how the alien's perspective/worldview differs from humans and whether that difference matters for the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the difference isn't important to plot or theme, simplify; if it is, use it to generate conflict, goals, and scenes that show that perspective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make them alien but not incomprehensible or just a human-mirror
rubrics_metrics.description: Aliens should feel 'other' while remaining comprehensible and not merely an aspect of humanity with a different skin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide enough detail for readers to sense alienness without making them baffling. Avoid mapping them wholly onto human archetypes or reducing them to a single trait.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remember: to an alien, humanity is all one race
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt the alien’s perspective: they will often not divide humans the way we do; human differences may be irrelevant to them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using this perspective can avoid projecting human in-group/out-group categories onto aliens and can produce interesting narrative friction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain what matters to the alien; show them pursuing goals
rubrics_metrics.description: Instead of trying to fully explain alien psychology, demonstrate what's important to them and show their attempts to achieve or defend it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ursula K. Le Guin is cited: present bizarre elements but make clear what the alien values, then let readers watch them try to get it — goals, losses, and striving are relatable even across species.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use protagonist POV to interpret alien behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Have your viewpoint character try to figure out and react to alien actions, which gives readers a bridge to understand and empathize.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The protagonist’s confusion/learning process is a natural way to reveal alien culture and make it emotionally accessible without heavy exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat races as full cultures (avoid one-note races)
rubrics_metrics.description: Give cultures multiple facets—history, social structure, food, naming conventions, diasporas, internal conflicts—rather than a single stereotyped trait.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resist shorthand (e.g., 'all dwarves are Gimli-like'); create internal variety and rules that inform behavior even if much of that detail remains off-page.

rubrics_metrics.name: Think through consequences of physiological/ecological differences
rubrics_metrics.description: If species have physical differences (scales, cold-bloodedness, extra limbs), work out how those traits affect housing, agriculture, social organization, and daily life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a scaled, cold-blooded 'horse' might require different stables or feeding; considering these consequences makes the world feel coherent and real.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't rename ordinary animals/races unless differences matter
rubrics_metrics.description: If a creature behaves just like an Earth analog, simply call it that rather than inventing a novelty name; reserve renaming for meaningful differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'when is a horse a horse' rule: only make it a 'zyloplick' (or similar) if its differences create story-relevant consequences or add genuine wonder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show sensory detail to create alienness and wonder
rubrics_metrics.description: Use sensory imagery (taste, smell, touch, wind in nostrils) to let readers experience how the alien perceives the world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small sensory moments can convey alien embodiment and create emotional resonance (e.g., 'let us taste grass'). This generates wonder and immediacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid film shorthand; exploit prose's ability for depth
rubrics_metrics.description: Film often uses quick shorthand for races (visual tropes, accents); prose has room to expand cultures beyond one-note portrayals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't rely on cinematic shortcuts; spend the effort to flesh out cultural complexity in writing where you have more space and time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know the rules behind cultural traits but avoid info-dumps
rubrics_metrics.description: Have internal rules and reasons for customs and behaviors so the culture feels real, but do not dump that entire background on the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep the worldbuilding in your notes; reveal only what serves scene and character, using implication and small consistent details rather than long exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be willing to make medium-based compromises and design shortcuts
rubrics_metrics.description: Different media (comics, prose, film) require different design choices (e.g., giving aliens eyebrows in comics to show expression).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept practical compromises to communicate quickly to the audience, but ensure those shortcuts don't undermine cultural coherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't invent races solely to fill a plot role; do the work to populate them
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid creating a race just to fulfill a narrative function and leaving it undeveloped; if a race fills a role, you must still flesh it out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you make a race to serve a particular plot purpose, follow through by thinking about how that role shapes culture, behavior, and interactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use small, consistent details to imply a deeper culture
rubrics_metrics.description: Let background design choices (naming irregularities, different naming conventions, foodstuffs, clan structures) surface as small details that imply larger systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even details that 'never make it into the story' can inform what does appear and give authenticity; readers pick up on consistent microevidence that a culture exists beyond the scene.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study exemplary works and techniques (learn from masters)
rubrics_metrics.description: Look to successful writers (e.g., Ursula K. Le Guin, Jane Yolen) for methods of rendering alienness and culture without losing relatability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use exemplary texts as models: Le Guin’s approach of showing what matters to an alien and the struggle to achieve it; Yolen’s mix of whimsy and realism are recommended as instructive examples.
